what_its_for: This medicine helps control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It combines two medicines in one pen: insulin degludec (a long-acting insulin) and liraglutide (a medicine that helps your body release insulin when needed and reduces appetite). It is used along with diet and exercise when other diabetes medicines have not worked well enough.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under the skin (subcutaneous injection) once a day. Inject it into your stomach area (abdomen), upper thigh, or upper arm. Rotate (change) your injection site each time to avoid skin problems. Do not inject into a vein or muscle. Always use a new needle for each injection. Do not shake the pen — gently roll it between your palms if you need to mix it. Read the Instructions for Use that come with your pen carefully before your first injection, and ask your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist to show you how to use it.
dosing: Your doctor will tell you exactly how many 'dose steps' to use each day. The starting dose is usually 10 dose steps (10 units of insulin / 0.36 mg of liraglutide) once a day. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose every week based on your blood sugar readings. The maximum dose is 50 dose steps per day. Take it at the same time every day — any time of day, with or without food. Do not change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and you remember the same day, take it as soon as you remember. Then go back to your regular schedule the next day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your usual time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Before first use: Store your unused pens in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze — throw the pen away if it has been frozen. After first use: Keep the pen at room temperature, below 86°F (30°C), or in the refrigerator. Use the pen within 21 days after first use, then throw it away even if medicine is still left. Always keep the pen cap on when not in use. Store away from direct heat and light. Keep this medicine and all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol or drink only in moderation, as alcohol can cause your blood sugar to drop too low (hypoglycemia). Do not drive or use heavy machinery if your blood sugar is low or if you are not sure how this medicine affects you. Avoid skipping meals, as this can cause low blood sugar. Do not share your pen or needles with anyone else — even if the needle is changed — as this can spread infection. Do not use this medicine with other GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines (such as Victoza, Ozempic, Trulicity) or other insulins unless your doctor tells you to. Avoid injecting into the same spot every time.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you have: signs of very low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) such as shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, dizziness, confusion, or fainting; signs of very high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision; severe stomach pain that does not go away (this could be a sign of pancreatitis — swelling of the pancreas); signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or trouble breathing; a lump, rash, or thickened skin at your injection site that does not go away; signs of kidney problems such as decreased urination or swelling in your legs or feet; a fast or pounding heartbeat or shortness of breath. Also tell your doctor if you are sick, have an infection, or are under unusual stress, as these can change your blood sugar levels.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working shortly after your first injection, but it may take several days to weeks to see your full blood sugar benefit. Because insulin degludec is a long-acting insulin, it builds up a steady level in your body over the first few days. Your doctor will check your blood sugar regularly and may adjust your dose over time. Continue taking this medicine even if you feel well — diabetes is a long-term condition that needs ongoing treatment.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): This medicine can be used in older adults, but your doctor may start with a lower dose and watch your blood sugar more carefully, as older adults may be more sensitive to low blood sugar. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how this medicine works in your body and your dose may need to be adjusted. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Controlling blood sugar during pregnancy is very important, but your doctor will decide the safest medicine for you. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in people under 18 years of age.
